title: Judge dismisses Chegg and Penske antitrust lawsuits targeting Google AI search
gist: Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Chegg and Penske antitrust suits over Google's AI overviews, holding that publishers' expectation of search traffic is not an agreement; he was sympathetic but said fairness must be addressed by legislation, leaving EU and UK regulators as the likelier venues.

themes.theme: Dismissal of Chegg and Penske suits

insights.claim: A US federal judge, Amit Mehta, dismissed the 2025 antitrust lawsuits brought by Chegg and Penske Media against Google over AI search products such as AI overviews, ruling Google's conduct is not illegal under antitrust law.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Removes a near-term US antitrust threat to Google's AI overviews rollout.

insights.claim: Chegg alleged Google illegally scraped its educational content so Gemini models could recreate it and cut the site's traffic; Penske alleged publishers indexed for organic search also have content harvested for AI answers with no opt-out.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Shows the core theory publishers use: search indexing is tied to AI harvesting with no opt-out.

insights.claim: The court held that publishers' expectation of search traffic in exchange for free content is not a legal agreement, so antitrust law does not apply absent a formal arrangement with Google.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Lacking a contract, publishers have weak antitrust footing against search-AI integration in US courts.
insights.quote: But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.
insights.locator: These arguments did not sway the judge

insights.claim: Judge Mehta acknowledged that Google's AI search approach may be unfair to publishers and harms journalists, educators and creators whose content is repurposed without compensation, yet held this is not illegal.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Reputational and political pressure on Google persists even after the legal win.
insights.quote: The court does not treat Plaintiffs' alleged harms lightly

insights.claim: The ruling says antitrust law cannot substitute for legislative action merely because an outcome feels unfair; economic harm from innovation is not automatically an illegal act.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Relief for publishers in the US likely requires new legislation rather than litigation.
insights.locator: This case essentially comes down to the nature of innovation

insights.claim: Mehta also presided over the DOJ's search antitrust case, found Google violated the law, but the government did not obtain the harsh penalties it sought.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Context: same judge has been comparatively restrained on remedies against Google.
insights.locator: And Mehta is aware of the legal issues

insights.claim: Further US legal challenges to Google's AI search face an uphill battle absent new legislation, and lawmakers have been slow to adapt to the AI era.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Low US legal risk for AI search near term; watch for legislative proposals.
insights.locator: Google will undoubtedly face more legal challenges

insights.claim: Publishers may fare better abroad: the European Commission is considering the same questions and tends to take a dimmer view of Big Tech, and the UK has ordered Google to provide an AI opt-out for sites that want to remain in organic search.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for Google AI search is concentrated in the EU and UK.
insights.locator: Publishers may have more luck overseas

insights.claim: Google is exploring paying sites directly for contributing to AI answers, but its pilot program is reportedly not going over well with publishers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: A licensing model is emerging but lacks publisher buy-in so far.
insights.locator: Google is exploring ways to pay sites
